patient.name: Marcus Delgado
patient.chiefComplaint: Gunshot wound to the left chest

history.hpi: Patient was standing outside a convenience store when he was shot once in the left anterior chest during an apparent robbery attempt. Bystanders called 911 immediately; police secured the scene prior to EMS entry. Patient was initially able to speak but is now increasingly short of breath and anxious.
history.events: Single gunshot wound sustained during attempted robbery; bystanders called 911, scene secured by police prior to EMS entry

scene.dispatch: 26-year-old male, gunshot wound, conscious and breathing, outside commercial building
scene.location: Sidewalk outside a convenience store, scene secured by police
scene.safety: Scene secured by law enforcement prior to EMS entry; shooter not apprehended, area remains monitored
scene.bystanders: Store clerk called 911, did not witness the shooting directly
visualCues: Single gunshot wound to left anterior chest, second intercostal space midclavicular line
Minimal external bleeding at wound site
Patient sitting upright, leaning forward, visibly dyspneic

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 26-year-old male sitting upright with a single gunshot wound to the left anterior chest. He is increasingly dyspneic with visible jugular venous distention and tracheal deviation.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking in short 3-4 word sentences
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Labored, asymmetric chest rise, diminished on the left
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses weak and rapid, skin pale
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all four extremities
otherFindings: Single GSW to left anterior chest, 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line
Absent breath sounds on the left

transitions.condition: Crew performs a MARCH primary survey, recognizes absent left breath sounds with JVD, tracheal deviation, and hypotension as tension pneumothorax, and performs immediate needle decompression of the left second intercostal space.

phases.name: Tension pneumothorax decompressed
phases.description: Crew recognizes the classic signs of tension pneumothorax and performs needle decompression of the left chest, with immediate improvement in breath sounds and hemodynamics.
phases.triggerCondition: After the primary survey identifies absent left breath sounds, JVD, tracheal deviation, and hypotension consistent with tension pneumothorax, the crew immediately performs needle decompression of the left second intercostal space at the midclavicular line.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Improved, more symmetric chest rise, breath sounds returning on the left
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all four extremities
otherFindings: Rush of air heard on decompression
Semi-occlusive dressing applied to chest wound

expectedActions.shortAction: Perform MARCH primary survey; identify absent left breath sounds, JVD, and hypotension
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If absent or diminished breath sounds in a hypotensive trauma patient, especially those with chest trauma and/or tracheal deviation, consider tension pneumothorax
expectedActions.rationale: Recognizing the triad of absent breath sounds, JVD, and hypotension is what drives urgent decompression.

expectedActions.shortAction: Needle decompression of left 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: perform needle decompression of side without breath sounds or side opposite tracheal deviation; may need second or third needle decompression on same side if there is a rush of air but patient again has symptoms
expectedActions.rationale: Immediate decompression relieves the obstructive physiology causing hypotension and hypoxia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply semi-occlusive dressing over the open chest wound
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For open chest wound, place semi-occlusive dressing
expectedActions.rationale: Prevents ongoing air entry through the chest wall wound while allowing trapped air to vent.

expectedActions.shortAction: Establish large-bore IV access; give 500 mL crystalloid bolus for SBP <90 mmHg
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Establish IV access if needed (large bore preferred). If SBP less than 90 mmHg or HR greater than 120 BPM, initiate resuscitation: consider 500 mL bolus of IV fluid, repeat as needed for persistent signs and symptoms of shock. Trauma resuscitation target SBP 90 mmHg
expectedActions.rationale: Supports perfusion while the obstructive component is being addressed.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 greater than 94%
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Monitor oxygen saturation (SpO2) and, if indicated, provide supplemental oxygen to maintain SPO2 greater than 94% and respiratory support if needed
expectedActions.rationale: Corrects hypoxia from the ventilation-perfusion mismatch caused by the pneumothorax.

transitions.condition: With the tension pneumothorax decompressed and hemodynamics improving, the crew packages the patient and initiates rapid transport to the trauma center with minimal scene time.
The crew focuses on IV access and fluid administration without recognizing or acting on the signs of tension pneumothorax, delaying needle decompression.

phases.name: Rapid transport initiated
phases.description: With the tension physiology resolved, the patient is packaged and transported rapidly to a trauma center with continued reassessment en route.
phases.triggerCondition: Following successful needle decompression, occlusive dressing, and IV access with fluid resuscitation, the patient's hemodynamics and breath sounds improve; the crew packages for rapid transport to a trauma center with minimized scene time.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Nonlabored, symmetric chest rise, breath sounds present bilaterally
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all four extremities
otherFindings: Repeat exam shows resolved tension physiology
Dressing intact, no active external bleeding
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Thank you, I feel a lot better."

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess breath sounds, vitals, and mental status serially en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Monitor patient for deterioration over time with serial vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) and repeat neurologic status assessment
expectedActions.rationale: Tension physiology can recur; repeat exam catches early recurrence before decompensation.

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport to trauma center; minimize scene time (goal under 10 minutes) for penetrating torso trauma
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patients with major hemorrhage, hemodynamic instability, penetrating torso trauma, or signs of traumatic brain injury often require rapid surgical intervention. Minimize scene time (goal is under 10 minutes) and initiate rapid transport to the highest level of care within the trauma system
expectedActions.rationale: Penetrating torso trauma requires surgical intervention that only a trauma center can provide.

phases.name: Decompression delayed
phases.description: The crew prioritizes IV access and fluids without recognizing the tension physiology. Intrathoracic pressure continues to rise, and the patient rapidly deteriorates toward obstructive shock.
phases.triggerCondition: The crew focuses on IV access and fluid administration without recognizing tension physiology; needle decompression is delayed, allowing intrathoracic pressure to continue rising.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Severely labored, absent breath sounds on the left, worsening tracheal deviation
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses weak, thready, barely palpable

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize worsening tension physiology; perform immediate needle decompression
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: perform needle decompression of side without breath sounds or side opposite tracheal deviation; may need second or third needle decompression on same side if there is a rush of air but patient again has symptoms
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed recognition allows obstructive shock to worsen; decompression remains the definitive rescue action.
